## Multi-layer dissolution ERGMs

A weighted network with weights $w_{ij}$ is cut into nested binary layers by
thresholds $t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_K$:
$$
x_k = \{ij : w_{ij} \ge t_k\}, \qquad x_0 \supseteq x_1 \supseteq \dots \supseteq x_K .
$$

Each transition $x_{k-1} \to x_k$ is modelled by an exponential random graph
model whose statistics $s(x_k)$ are computed on layer $k$, conditionally on the
observed lower layers $\tilde x_{k-1}$:
$$
p(x_{1:K} \mid \tilde x_{0:K-1}, \varphi_{1:K}) \propto
\exp\left\{\sum_{k=1}^K \varphi_k^\top s(x_k)\right\}
\prod_{k=1}^K 1\{x_k \subseteq \tilde x_{k-1}\}.
$$

Layer $k$ can only keep edges of the observed layer below it, so $\varphi_k$
describes which edges survive the $k$-th threshold: a dissolution process
across the weight scale. When every edge of $x_0$ also carries a sign $z_{ij}$
(in gene co-expression networks, for instance, the sign of the correlation
between two genes), the signs are modelled jointly with the layers, and the
statistics $s(z, x_k)$ can distinguish positive and negative edges:
$$
p(z, x_{1:K} \mid \tilde x_{0:K-1}, \varphi_{1:K}) \propto
\exp\left\{\sum_{k=1}^K \varphi_k^\top s(z, x_k)\right\}
\prod_{k=1}^K 1\{x_k \subseteq \tilde x_{k-1}\}.
$$

In both cases the layer parameters are partially pooled by a hierarchical
prior,
$$
\varphi_k \mid \mu, \Sigma \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma), \quad
\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \Sigma_0), \quad \Sigma \sim \mathrm{IW}(\nu_0, S_0),
$$
so that $\mu$ is the effect common to all layers and $\Sigma$ measures how much
the layers differ. `bergm_w()` fits the model without signs and `bergm_ws()`
the model with signs; both sample the posterior
$\pi(\varphi, \mu, \Sigma \mid y)$ with the adaptive exchange algorithm of
Section 5.

The code below uses the names of the notation:

| notation | meaning | code |
|---|---|---|
| $w_{ij}$, $t_0, \dots, t_K$, $z_{ij}$ | weights, thresholds, signs | `w`, `t_k`, `z` |
| $y = (z, x_{0:K})$ | observed signed network | `y` |
| $x = x_{0:K}$ | observed network without signs | `x` |
| $s(z, x_k)$, $s(x_k)$ | statistics, as an **ergm.multi** formula | `s`, `s_x` |
| $\mu_0, \Sigma_0, \nu_0, S_0$ | hyperparameters | `mu0`, `Sigma0`, `nu0`, `S0` |
| $\pi(\varphi, \mu, \Sigma \mid y)$ | posterior | `post`, `post_x` |
| $\varphi_k$, $\mu$ | layer parameters, hierarchical mean | `phi`, `mu` |
| $y'$ | auxiliary network of the exchange algorithm | (internal) |
| $y^{\mathrm{rep}}$ | networks simulated from either prior or posterior predictive distribution | `y_prior`, `y_rep`, `x_rep` |

## 2. Simulated data

`toy_ws` is a network on 40 nodes simulated
with `ws_simulate(n = 40, seed = 33)`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
data(toy_ws)

w <- toy_ws$weights

t_k <- toy_ws$thresholds

z <- toy_ws$signs

y <- ws_data(w, t_k, z); y
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Signed weighted network: 40 nodes, K = 3 layer transitions (x_0 -> x_3)

 layer threshold edges positive negative % positive triangles % +++
   x_0    0.6995   234      180       54       76.9       717  61.1
   x_1    0.8341   129      112       17       86.8       190  79.5
   x_2    0.9164    65       61        4       93.8        41  82.9
   x_3    0.9576    33       32        1       97.0         8  75.0
```


:::
:::



The share of positive edges grows with the weight, as it often does in real
co-expression networks: strong interactions are mostly positive.



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
xy <- ws_layout(y)
plot(y, layout = xy)
```

:::
:::



## 3. Weighted signed networks: `bergm_ws()`

### Model specification

The statistics are written as an **ergm.multi** formula. The layers are called
`x_1`, `x_2`, `x_3` and the signs `z`, so `(z & x_k)` selects the positive
edges of layer $k$ and `(!z & x_k)` its negative edges. Every layer has the
same three statistics:



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
s <- ~ # layer 1
       L(~edges, ~(z & x_1)) + 
       L(~gwdegree(0.5, fixed = TRUE), ~(z & x_1)) +
       L(~edges, ~(!z & x_1)) +
       # layer 2
       L(~edges, ~(z & x_2)) +
       L(~gwdegree(0.5, fixed = TRUE), ~(z & x_2)) +
       L(~edges, ~(!z & x_2)) +
       # layer 3
       L(~edges, ~(z & x_3)) +
       L(~gwdegree(0.5, fixed = TRUE), ~(z & x_3)) +
       L(~edges, ~(!z & x_3))

model <- ws_model(y, s)
model
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Multi-layer dissolution ERGM for signed weighted networks
  layers (transitions): 3   statistics per layer: 3 
  formula:
    L(~edges, ~(z & x_1)) + L(~gwdegree(0.5, fixed = TRUE), ~(z & x_1)) + L(~edges,
      ~(!z & x_1)) + L(~edges, ~(z & x_2)) + L(~gwdegree(0.5, fixed = TRUE), ~(z &
      x_2)) + L(~edges, ~(!z & x_2)) + L(~edges, ~(z & x_3)) + L(~gwdegree(0.5, fixed =
      TRUE), ~(z & x_3)) + L(~edges, ~(!z & x_3))

Observed statistics :
        edges+ gwdeg+ edges-
layer 1    112  57.20     17
layer 2     61  50.82      4
layer 3     32  40.14      1
```


:::
:::



The same formula can be written once, as a template in which `x_k` stands for
every layer:
`~ L(~edges, ~(z & x_k)) + L(~gwdegree(0.5, fixed = TRUE), ~(z & x_k)) + L(~edges, ~(!z & x_k))`.

`ws_model()` checks the formula before anything is fitted: every statistic
must use exactly one layer, the statistics must be grouped by layer (all those
of `x_1` first) and every layer must have the same number of statistics,
because the hierarchical prior pools the $j$-th statistic of all layers. A
formula that breaks one of these rules is rejected with an explanation, and
statistics that are zero in the data or whose change statistics are nearly
collinear are reported.

The two edge terms set the baseline log-odds that a positive or a negative edge
of layer $k-1$ survives into layer $k$. The geometrically weighted degree term
describes how the surviving positive edges are spread over the nodes: a
negative coefficient means that they concentrate on nodes that already have
many positive edges, a positive one that they are spread evenly.

### Prior specification



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior <- ws_prior(model, 
                  mu0 = 0, 
                  Sigma0 = 3, 
                  nu0 = model$p + 9, 
                  S0 = 1)

prior
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Hierarchical prior (p = 3 statistics per layer)
  mu ~ N(mu0, Sigma0), Sigma ~ inverse-Wishart(nu0 = 12, S0)
  prior mean of mu0: 0.00, 0.00, 0.00 
  prior sd of mu: 1.73, 1.73, 1.73 
  expected between-layer sd, sqrt(diag(E[Sigma])): 0.35, 0.35, 0.35 
```


:::
:::



These are the default values: $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 3I)$ and
$\Sigma \sim \mathrm{IW}(p + 9, I)$, so that the expected between-layer standard
deviation is about 0.35. With few layers $\Sigma$ is informed mostly by the
prior, which acts as a moderate shrinkage of the layers towards each other. A
prior predictive check shows the networks the prior considers plausible:



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
y_prior <- ws_predictive(model, 
                         prior = prior, 
                         type = "prior", 
                         nsim = 100,
                         seed = 1, 
                         verbose = FALSE)
plot(y_prior)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Bergm.ws_files/figure-html/prior-pred-1.png){fig-align='center' width=825}
:::
:::





Every observed statistic lies inside the central 95% of the prior predictive distribution: the prior is weakly informative on the scale of the data.

### Posterior inference



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
post <- bergm_ws(model, 
                 prior = prior, 
                 n_iter = 15000, 
                 burnin = 1500, 
                 n_chains = 3,
                 cores = 2, 
                 seed = 2026, 
                 verbose = FALSE)
```
:::



The same fit is obtained in one call with `bergm_ws(y, s, ...)`; building the
model first lets us look at it and at the prior before fitting. The four chains
start from dispersed points, adapt their proposal during the burn-in and then
share the same frozen proposal.



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary_post <- summary(post)
summary_post
```

### Results

The posterior means of $\varphi_k$ (one row per layer) and of $\mu$:



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
phi <- coef(post)
mu <- coef(post, what = "mu")
round(phi, 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
        edges+ gwdeg+ edges-
layer 1   0.76  -1.98  -1.02
layer 2   0.71  -1.20  -1.30
layer 3   0.67  -0.59  -1.37
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
round(mu, 2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
edges+ gwdeg+ edges- 
  0.70  -1.23  -1.22 
```


:::
:::



The interval plot shows every effect in every layer next to the hierarchical
mean:



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(post, type = "intervals")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Bergm.ws_files/figure-html/intervals-1.png){fig-align='center' width=880}
:::
:::



Positive edges are more likely than negative ones to survive into the next
layer in every layer. The degree effect of the positive edges is negative
(posterior means -1.98, -1.20
and -0.59 in layers 1 to 3): the positive edges that
survive concentrate on nodes with many positive edges, which in this network
are the cores of the modules. The effect weakens as the threshold rises, and
the hierarchical prior pulls the three layers towards the common mean.



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(post, max_points = 500)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Bergm.ws_files/figure-html/traces-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1100}
:::
:::



The four chains overlap after the burn-in.

### Posterior predictive checks

Posterior predictive networks are compared with the observed one on the model
statistics and on statistics the model does not contain: the four kinds of
signed triangles and the spread of the positive degrees in every layer.



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
y_rep <- ws_predictive(post, nsim = 200, seed = 2, verbose = FALSE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(y_rep, what = "model")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Bergm.ws_files/figure-html/post-pred-1.png){fig-align='center' width=825}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(y_rep, what = "gof")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Bergm.ws_files/figure-html/post-pred-2.png){fig-align='center' width=825}
:::
:::



The model describes how many positive and negative edges survive
and how they are spread over the nodes, but contains no term for triangles, so
statistics of triangle closure are where it is most likely to fail. A natural
extension adds a shared-partner term to every layer, for instance
`gwespL(0.5, fixed = TRUE, L.base = ~(z & x_k), Ls.path = list(~(z & x_k), ~(z & x_k)))`
for positive triangles (labelled `gwesp+++`), usually with `scale = "gwesp"`
so that its coefficient is comparable across layers.

Finally, `ws_aux_check()` compares auxiliary networks of the length used by the
sampler with networks from chains twenty times longer, at the posterior mean:

ws_aux_check(post, seed = 3)

## 4. Weighted networks (without signs): `bergm_w()`

When edges have weights but no signs, `bergm_w()` fits the model of Section 1
without $z$ (Caimo and Gollini, 2020). The formula uses the layers `x_1`, ...,
`x_K`, or `x_k` in a template; any term can be applied to a layer with `L()`,
for example `L(~edges, ~x_k)`, `L(~triangle, ~x_k)`,
`L(~gwdegree(0.5, fixed = TRUE), ~x_k)` or `L(~nodematch("module"), ~x_k)`, and
shared partners with
`gwespL(0.5, fixed = TRUE, L.base = ~x_k, Ls.path = list(~x_k, ~x_k))`.
Setting $t_0$ below the smallest weight makes $x_0$ the set of all observed
edges.

We use the weights of `toy_ws` and ignore the signs:



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- ws_data(w, t_k, attributes = toy_ws$attributes)
x
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Node attributes: module, pathway

   x_1    0.8341   129       190        6.45
   x_2    0.9164    65        41        3.25

```

of Section 3 also asks how the signs of the edges relate to their weights.

## 5. The adaptive exchange algorithm







The normalising constant $c(\varphi)$ of the multi-layer model on the observed
supports is intractable, so the likelihood ratio of a Metropolis–Hastings step
cannot be computed. The exchange algorithm (Murray et al., 2006; Caimo and
Friel, 2011) simulates an auxiliary network $y'$ at the proposed value
$\varphi'$; with $y'$ in the acceptance ratio, $c(\varphi)$ and $c(\varphi')$
cancel and the likelihood ratio is replaced by
$\exp\{(\varphi' - \varphi)^\top (s(y) - s(y'))\}$. The auxiliary network is
drawn by `aux_iters` steps of the **ergm** sampler started at the observed
network (by default ten proposals per dyad-layer pair that can change, and at
least 2,000); `ws_aux_check()` checks that this is long enough.

The basic sampler alternates an exchange step for $\varphi$ with Gibbs draws of
$\mu$ and $\Sigma$. **Bergm.ws** improves it in four ways, none of which changes
the posterior.

**1. Starting values and proposal from the Fisher information.** The chains
start at the penalised maximum pseudo-likelihood estimate, the mode of the
logistic pseudo-likelihood times the Gaussian prior of $\varphi$ (with $\Sigma$
at its prior mean), which is finite even when a statistic separates the dyads.
Two moment-matching Newton steps then move towards the posterior mode,

$$
\varphi \leftarrow \varphi + (I_\varphi + P)^{-1}
\{s(y) - \mathrm{E}_\varphi s - P(\varphi - m)\},
$$

where $\mathrm{E}_\varphi s$ and the Fisher information $I_\varphi$ are the mean
and covariance of `n_info` networks simulated at $\varphi$, and $P$ and $m$ the
prior precision and mean of $\varphi$. The initial proposal covariance is
$B_0 = (I_\varphi + P)^{-1}$ and the initial scale $2.38/\sqrt{2d}$ for
$d = Kp$ parameters: the usual random-walk scale, reduced by $\sqrt 2$ because
the exchange step adds noise of about the same size as the log-likelihood
ratio.

**2. Delayed acceptance.** The score $g = s(y) - \mathrm{E}_c s$ and information
$H = I_c$ at the starting value $c$ define a Gaussian surrogate of the
log-likelihood,
$\tilde\ell(\varphi) = g^\top(\varphi - c) - \tfrac12 (\varphi - c)^\top H (\varphi - c)$.
Each proposal first passes a cheap test with the surrogate and the exact prior;
only then is the auxiliary network simulated, and a second test corrects for
the surrogate (Christen and Fox, 2005):

$$
\alpha_1 = \min\left\{1, \exp\{\tilde\ell(\varphi') - \tilde\ell(\varphi)\}
\frac{p(\varphi')}{p(\varphi)}\right\}, \qquad
\alpha_2 = \min\left\{1, 
\frac{\exp\left\{(\varphi' - \varphi)^\top \left[s(y) - s(y')\right]\right\}}
     {\exp\left\{\tilde\ell(\varphi') - \tilde\ell(\varphi)\right\}}\right\}.
$$

**3. The hierarchical mean integrated out.** When the layers move together,
$\varphi$ and $\mu$ are strongly dependent and the plain Gibbs scheme is slow.
Given $\Sigma$, $\mu$ is integrated out analytically,
$$
\varphi \mid \Sigma \sim \mathcal{N}\big(1_K \otimes \mu_0,\;
I_K \otimes \Sigma + J_K \otimes \Sigma_0\big),
$$
with $J_K$ the $K \times K$ matrix of $1$s. The exchange step uses this prior
(`collapse_mu = TRUE`); $\mu$ is then drawn from $\mathcal{N}(m_\mu, S_\mu)$ with
$S_\mu = (\Sigma_0^{-1} + K\Sigma^{-1})^{-1}$ and
$m_\mu = S_\mu(\Sigma_0^{-1}\mu_0 + K\Sigma^{-1}\bar\varphi)$, and $\Sigma$
from $\mathrm{IW}(\nu_0 + K, S_0 + \sum_k (\varphi_k - \mu)(\varphi_k - \mu)^\top)$:
a partially collapsed Gibbs sampler (van Dyk and Park, 2008).

**4. Adaptation in three phases.** During the burn-in the proposal covariance
is re-estimated as $0.95\,\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}} + 0.05\,B_0$ from the second
half of the chain's history (Haario et al., 2001), and the scale is tuned
towards an acceptance rate of 0.234. With several chains
(`pool_adaptation = TRUE`), each chain adapts on its own during the first three
quarters of the burn-in; the within-chain covariances are then averaged and
given to every chain, which only tunes the scale during the last quarter;
finally the scale is set to the geometric mean over the chains and the
proposal is frozen. The retained draws of all chains come from the same Markov
kernel. With `update = "layer"` the step is repeated for each layer in turn, with one
auxiliary network per layer.

### Technical improvements over the basic exchange sampler

The comparison below fits a signed model of `toy_ws` with 15 parameters,
```r
s <- ~ L(~edges, ~(z & x_k)) + 
       L(~nodematch("pathway"), ~(z & x_k)) + 
       L(~edges, ~(!z & x_k)) +
          gwespL(0.5, 
                 fixed = TRUE, 
                 L.base = ~(z & x_k), 
                 Ls.path = list(~(z & x_k), ~(z & x_k))) +
          gwespL(0.5, 
                 fixed = TRUE, 
                 L.base = ~(!z & x_k), 
                 Ls.path = list(~(z & x_k), ~(z & x_k)))
```

with `scale = "gwesp"`, 4 chains of 4,000 iterations (1,000 of burn-in) on
2 cores, adding the improvements one at a time, for two seeds.
All four samplers share the starting values and initial proposal of
improvement 1. These runs take about half an hour, so their results are stored
with the package; the script that produced them is
`system.file("scripts", "precompute_vignettes.R", package = "Bergm.ws")`.

|sampler              | seconds|simulated | acceptance| median ESS| min ESS| max Rhat| ESS/min|
|:--------------------|-------:|:---------|----------:|----------:|-------:|--------:|-------:|
|basic                |     268|100%      |       0.23|         92|      52|     1.47|    20.6|
|+ delayed acceptance |     113|39%       |       0.26|         61|      37|     1.49|    32.5|
|+ mu integrated out  |     113|37%       |       0.20|        101|      63|     1.40|    53.5|

"Simulated" is the share of proposals that needed an auxiliary network, ESS the
effective sample size over all chains of $\varphi$ and $\mu$, and the columns
are averages over the two seeds. Delayed acceptance simulates a network for
fewer than half of the proposals and raises the effective sample size per
minute by a factor of 1.6; integrating out $\mu$
adds a further factor of 1.6. Pooling the
adaptation does not change the efficiency much, but it gives all chains the
same kernel and, in these runs, the lowest $\hat R$. All $\hat R$ values are
above 1.05 because the runs are deliberately short: they compare samplers, not
final analyses.

### Practical advice

- Write the formula with the same terms in the same order in every layer (a
  template with `x_k` does this automatically), and look at the model before
  fitting: nearly collinear statistics are better dropped than fitted with
  longer chains.
- Use at least four chains and look at $\hat R$ and the effective sample sizes;
  with `cores > 1` the chains run in parallel.

| argument | when/how to change it |
|---|---|
| `n_iter`, `burnin` | increase until $\hat R < 1.05$ and the effective sample sizes exceed a few hundred |
| `cores` | set to the number of chains if the machine allows |
| `aux_iters` | increase if `ws_aux_check()` finds differences |
| `update` | `"layer"` when the layer parameters are nearly uncorrelated a posteriori (see `summary(post)$corr`) |
| `delayed` | do not switch it off! |
| `dispersion` | larger values give a stricter convergence check |
